Description: Respondents reported very low rates of adverse experiences after mescaline use; no specific types, counts, or denominator given in this article
CEQ (Challenging Experiences Questionnaire) total-sample mean score 0.6 (SD 0.7) of 5, indicating low-intensity in-session challenging effects
Sweating at 24h in one patient, resolved by 48h; also present in a separate treatment-failure case with persistent withdrawal signs.
Chills present at 24 and 48h in one abstinent patient; also occurred in a separate treatment-failure case with persistent withdrawal.
Nausea reported in the treatment-failure case and in the fatal case ~17h post-ibogaine, ~2h before respiratory arrest; no intervention documented.
Muscle aches reported in the treatment-failure case and in the fatal case at 17h post-ibogaine; no intervention documented.
Dilated pupils (mydriasis) observed in the treatment-failure case as part of persistent objective opioid-withdrawal signs post-ibogaine.
Respiratory arrest ~18h post-ibogaine (29 mg/kg) in a 24-year-old female; pronounced dead ~19h post-treatment; cause of death undetermined.
Fatal acute ibogaine intoxication (single-agent or with non-drug comorbid contributing factors, e.g. cardiovascular disease); death within hours of ingestion.
Fatal multidrug intoxication combining ibogaine with opioids (morphine, methadone, fentanyl), cocaine, and/or benzodiazepines (diazepam); death within hours of ingestion.
Fatal cardiac event (myocardial infarction, arrhythmia, or cardiorespiratory arrest) as proximate or contributing cause of death, often with preexisting cardiovascular disease.
Suspected fatal pulmonary thromboembolism per clinical/death-certificate diagnosis; autopsy inadequate to confirm in any of the three cases.
Witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure c. 17h post-ingestion, possibly related to alcohol/benzodiazepine withdrawal, in a case that was ultimately fatal.
Acute hemorrhagic pancreatitis complicating chronic alcoholism, fatal, occurring during ibogaine treatment.
Hemorrhagic complications of duodenal ulcer, possibly with increased intracranial pressure from ventricular obstruction; fatal outcome.
Physical symptoms: disrupted vision, temperature dysregulation, numbness/tingling, insomnia, GI distress, reduced appetite, increased migraines/headaches (18.0%, 108.5 reports).
Impaired focus: poor concentration, distractibility, absent-mindedness reported by microdosers (8.8%, 53 of 603.5 coded challenge reports).
Increased anxiety (general, social, existential) reported as a microdosing drawback (6.7%, 40.5 of 603.5 coded challenge reports).
Impaired energy: restlessness/jitters (excess) or fatigue/drowsiness/brain fog (inadequate) reported (7.2%, 43.5 of 603.5 coded challenge reports).
Impaired mood: sadness, discontent, irritability, mood swings, fear, feeling unusual reported as a drawback (6.9%, 41.5 of 603.5 reports).
Social interference: awkwardness, oversharing, difficulty with sentence production in social settings (2.6%, 15.5 of 603.5 coded reports).
Cognitive interference: confusion, disorientation, racing thoughts, poor memory reported as a challenge (2.3%, 14 of 603.5 coded reports).
Self-interference: dissociation, depersonalization, rumination/over-analysis reported as a challenge (1.2%, 7.5 of 603.5 coded reports).
Increased symptoms: concerns re: psychological dependence/addiction potential, substance tolerance, comedown/hangover after effects (part of 6.2%, 37.5 reports).
Rare "adverse psychological events" noted by authors within increased-symptoms category; no further detail given (0.7% of coded challenges).
